quotes.text: Attempting to neutralize the opponent's competitive advantage, their first hire was a British citizen with musical stage experience. From there they added three Americans who met the specs, hired Boyce and Hart to write a bunch of pop songs, session men to play the instruments and allowed the more vocally-inclined cast members to sing along to the backing tracks.
By the third album, Headquarters, The Monkees were pretty much in control of the musical product and eventually wound up self-producing their work.

I give Mike Nesmith and Peter Tork a lot of credit for leading the revolt against the producers for creative control of their music because it would have been much easier simply to let the music manufacturing machine run until it ran out of gas and rake in as much cash as they could.

The first post-coup album, Headquarters, shows some promise and one stunning song. After that, the band began to splinter, eventually winding up in a situation similar to The Beatles on Abbey Road: each individual band member would show up separately to record their parts and leave.
This lack of collaborative spirit led to an ongoing reliance on session musicians, opening themselves up to continuing criticism that they still weren't a real band.

while TV producers Bob Rafelson and Bert Schneider weren't too worried about finding guys for their TV show band who actually had any musical talent, they were smart enough to get the best commercial songwriters the industry had to offer to crank out songs for them. We're talking Carol "Tapestry" King, along with Gerry "I used to be married to Carol King" Goffin, and Tommy Boyce and Bobby Hart, and Leiber and Stoller, and Neil Sedaka, and even Neil Freakin' Diamond. The cream of the Brill Building crop. These were ace songwriters, and for all the well deserved scorn that gets heaped on the Monkees' lack of musical ability, the songs themselves were absolutely fantastic for all the years they had their TV show (not so much after, though). Sure, they were bubblegum, but it must be said that it was exceptionally high quality bubble gum, and who doesn't like good bubblegum?

while they weren't the most artistically gifted guys on the planet, they at least had the desire to be taken seriously as artists, and props for that, your average Disney Channel TV band doesn't give two craps about making good music. But the Monkees did, so much that they went toe to toe with their producers and wrested some artistic control for themselves on their third album, Headquarters. They wanted to be more than the manufactured hyped-up phony band that they were, and actually put some effort into trying to become more, and if you ask me, there's something to be said for that.

After their TV series ended, the Monkees thought it would be a good idea to try and gain some artistic credibility through torpedoing their bubblegum image by making a radically hip, groovy, far out movie. So to generate ideas for their groovy movie, they sat around smoking pot with producer Bob Rafelson and newfound chum Jack Nicholson (true story!) and brainstormed ideas, and it turned out pretty much like you'd expect a movie written while smoking weed with Jack Nicholson to turn out.

Not that it was it intended to be. The Suits behind The Monkees weren't particularly interested in making a classic album. What they actually interested in was rushing product out as quickly as possible to capitalize on the success of the TV series and (more lucratively) the success of The Monkees' first album.

But then considering the exploitive nature of the whole enterprise, you have to give The Suits credit, they did enlist some of the best songwriters the Brill Building had to offer, when they could have had just about anybody write songs and sold the album on image alone.
So The Monkees did have better material than The Suits really had to give them if they were just trying to sell records to 12 year old girls.

I think great music is great music no matter where it comes from, and if all that The Monkees did was show up at the studio and sing a great song, it's still a great song worth listening to whether or not they wrote it or played on it or had anything else at all to do with it.
The bulk of the songwriting on the album was farmed out to professional songwriters, and some of them were superb.

Michael Nesmith gives us a winner with "Mary Mary". Don Kirschner seems to have been willing to give Nesmith one song per album on those early releases, and this one's great. They probably should have had him write a bunch more songs for the album, it would have been a better album maybe.

It was the first album on which the group members made substantial songwriting and instrumental contributions, rather than relying on session musicians and professional songwriters. After a struggle for creative autonomy with their record label, the group had been allowed, to a degree, to record by themselves.

It was released on November 6, 1967, when the Monkees were exerting more control over their music and had started to play many of the instruments themselves, something that their record company had previously forbidden. However, though the group had full control over the album, they invited more contributions from outside songwriters than on their previous album, Headquarters, and used session musicians to complement their sound.
The album also featured some of the earliest uses of the Moog synthesizer in popular music.
